structureTypeSource: Pitts S-2B: welded 4130 steel-tube fuselage, fabric covered; wooden wings (FAA TCDS A8SO; Aviat S-2B maintenance manual).
_wingStructureNote: Contact damage (Ty 2026-11-03). Break stations = the I-strut attach on each wing and the aileron slave struts 10 in (0.254 m) inboard of them: tools/own_models/build_pitts_s2b.py v11/v12 (YI_U 2.28, YI_L 2.18, Y_SL_U/L). The stick drives the LOWER ailerons and the uppers follow through the struts (Ty: with the lower panel gone the upper aileron trails stick free).

slaveStrut.source: Horns (2026-11-03): each aileron's horn runs FORWARD of its hinge line, inside the fixed wing's trailing-edge cove, its pin a little BELOW the chord line, and the strut passes through a slot in the skin (the lower wing's top skin; S-2s with symmetrical ailerons carry a small fairing over it). Pitts S-1-11 factory drawing Detail A (11-510-53 aileron link fork on an AN3-6 bolt, ahead of the 11-460 lower aileron's nose; biplaneforum.com 'Pitts S1-11 slave struts' thread 20836): measured off that unscaled section, the hinge-to-pin line runs ~20 deg below the chord, forward. The upper horn is made parallel and equal to it: owners rig the four ailerons to move together and 'the bends in the arms line up the two arcs' (biplaneforum thread 19463), i.e. a parallelogram, which moves the uppers 1:1 with the lowers. Arm 0.072 m (2.8 in) kept from the builder's pin offset; no published S-2 arm length found (Aviat S-2B parts catalogue not reachable). The old model's horns pointed opposite ways vertically (lower one standing ABOVE the lower wing), which across the strut's stagger lean moved the uppers at ~0.1 of the lowers (StrutStationTests).

mass.inertiaSource: Ixx/Iyy/Izz/Ixz kg.m2 about the CG. DERIVED 2026-11-02, docs/aircraft/pitts-s2b-inertia-DERIVATION.md (part-by-part build-up, which gave 401/1048/1272/12 and replaced 660/1121/1341/50), then TRIMMED 2026-11-09 at the owner's direction - "reduce the inertia of the pitts a bit it might be overstated" - against the Roskam Part V bands the derivation itself validates to, per axis rather than uniformly. IZZ 1272 -> 1185: the build-up's R_z was 0.466 against the band's 0.38-0.45, and 1185 is exactly its 0.45 ceiling (k_z 1.268 m). IYY 1048 -> 1000, -4.6 %: R_y 0.460 against a 0.35-0.40 band, but the derivation gives a real reason to sit high (a 174 kg engine and a 36 kg propeller 1.1-1.6 m ahead of the CG with both occupants behind it, on a 5.19 m airframe), so this is only the build-up's own stated uncertainty - tails 25 % heavier moved Iyy 3 %, the engine CG fraction +-0.05 m is +-12 kg.m2 - and NOT forced into the band, which would want 794. IXX UNCHANGED at 401: R_x 0.24 is already BELOW the 0.25 floor, so roll has nothing to give, and the owner had reported "way too much" roll in the spin, which a lower Ixx would worsen. Net effect on the spin: Izz-Ixx goes 871 -> 784, -10 %, so the inertial couple that holds a spin flat is 10 % weaker. THEN the interplane I-struts halved 2026-11-10 at the owner's direction - "It could be the weights of the I struts on the wings I had them set to something like 6 lb each ... Try reducing their weight by 50% and double check the location against the 3 view drawing". 7.0 kg -> 3.5 kg (3.9 lb each) in the build-up, which moves the raw tensor 400/1048/1272/11.0 -> 393/1049/1264/10.5, and the same ratios applied to the trimmed numbers give 394/1000/1178/11. REVERTED 2026-11-10, same day, at his direction after flying it - "Bring back the I strut inertia" - so the tensor is 401/1000/1185/11 again and the struts are 7.0 kg. The halving was never going to do what it was asked to do and it was measured saying so before it shipped (Izz - Ixx is 784 either way); it is back because he wants the mass there, not because the arithmetic changed. LOCATION CHECKED and left alone: the GLB's Strut_Interplane box ends at |y| 2.299 m (upper station 2.28, lower 2.18 in build_pitts_s2b.py, both marked as his own v11/v12 review), which is 75 % of the 3.047 m upper semi-span the same mesh measures, and the mass table already used 2.30. NOTE WHAT THIS CANNOT DO: Izz - Ixx is 784 before and after, because a strut sits at a |y| that counts the same into both - so this does not touch the inertial couple that holds a flat spin, and it is not why a PARE recovery takes too long. Moving the struts 0.5 m inboard as well would take only 14 kg.m2 off each of Ixx and Izz, again cancelling in the difference.

surfaces._comment: 2026-11-02 (lane/claude-pitts-spin): the root strip (area 0.299 at z -0.237, all of it ABOVE the stab at z -0.071) is split at the stab plane. Aviat factory three-view as traced in tools/own_models/build_pitts_s2b.py (RTE, hinge H_T -3.30): the rudder runs from 0.32 m below the stab hinge plane to 0.85 m above it; 0.150 m2 of its 0.485 m2 (31 %) is BELOW the stab, centroid 0.089 m below the body axis (z +0.089), and the band from the stab up to the next strip is 0.133 m2, centroid z -0.198. The strip's authored 0.299 m2 is kept and shared in that 0.150 : 0.133 ratio; leading edge kept at x -3.270.

construction._comment: Crash-in-water damage (Core/Wreck, lane/claude-crash-water 2026-11-02). Welded steel-tube fuselage, wooden wings, doped fabric covering. Both cockpits under ONE acrylic canopy, measured from the own model (tools/own_models/build_pitts_s2b.py: X_CF/X_CA windscreen base -0.13 to rear bow -1.60, width from sill_w): plan area integrated over the sills 0.976 m2, mean width 0.664 m.

crossflow._camberNote: Sideslip -> nose down (owner Ty, 2026-11-01: "The Pitts is similar but less pronounced"). Same mechanism as the Extra's; this type had no camber keys at all, so the effect was absent rather than reduced. Areas and stations are the Extra's scaled by this airframe's own geometry (sideArea 4.442 vs 6.064, length 5.189 vs 6.942, measured from each type's sideCenterX); the coefficients are then lower again, 0.6 and 0.35 against 1.0 and 0.6, because the S-2B's turtledeck is rounder and shallower than the Extra's. Together that is about a third of the Extra's pitching moment at the same speed and sideslip. NOT measured against a wind tunnel: this is a feel number, and it is Ty's to move.

spinAero.finSidewashKSource: Strength of the fuselage crossflow acceleration at the vertical tail, amp = 1 + k*(R/r)^2 on each vertical strip's LATERAL flow. FITTED 2026-11-09 to the owner's "Build it so I can test the rudder crossflow fix", after "The rudder is much more effective in real life during spin recovery". At 0.5 the Pitts BOTH holds a developed upright flat spin (alpha 78.9, r -4.67 at entry) AND RECOVERS from it on Beggs-Mueller - idle, hands off, full opposite rudder brings it to alpha -3.1 and r 0.27 within 15 s, which is the first recovery this model has managed. It raises the fin's own working dynamic pressure from eta_t 0.10-0.47 to 0.46-1.40, which is where the authority comes from: the rudder's moment is dCN*q*S, so this escapes the arithmetic wall that defeated three attempts at reshaping the fin's CN curve (tools/aircraft_builder/fin_section.py). SWEEP: 0.3 does not spin at all (entry collapses to alpha 13); 0.5 spins and recovers; 0.7 spins at alpha 75.8 and recovers; 1.0 recovers but flattens to only alpha 66. COUPLED WITH stabHighAlphaK, and this is the trade to know: the recovery needs BOTH 1.9 of stab and 0.5 of sidewash. At stabHighAlphaK 1.3 the attitude is the owner's target 80.5 but it does NOT recover; at 1.9 it recovers and the flat spin sits at 77.3 instead of 80. Recovery costs about 3 degrees of flat-spin attitude, and which he wants is his call in the air. RAISED 0.5 -> 0.9 on 2026-11-10 after he flew it: "Good test it passed the beggs mueler albeit slower than the real airplane". Timed properly for the first time (BeggsTimingProbe, BEGGS_T=1), 0.5 took 6.90 TURNS and 12.7 s to stop rotating, where the real aeroplane stops inside a turn or two. The elevator cannot be the fix: hands-off it floats to its AFT stop and stays there, which is his own report of the real aeroplane ("stick stayed full aft") and therefore right - so the recovery has to come from the rudder with the stick pegged aft, exactly as he said on 2026-11-09 ("The rudder is much more effective in real life during spin recovery"). Sweep at stabHighAlphaK 1.9 with controlSpoilerK 0.6: 0.5 -> 7.53 turns at alpha 78.9, 0.7 -> 4.85 at 77.6, 0.9 -> 3.14 at 76.3, 1.2 -> will not hold a flat spin at all (collapses to alpha 32). 0.9 is the last value that still spins, and it more than halves the recovery. THE TRADE, at 0.9: stabHighAlphaK 1.4 gives his 80 deg attitude and 5.12 turns, 1.6 gives 78.7 and 4.15, 1.9 gives 76.3 and 3.14, 2.2 gives 74.8 and 2.67. Shipped at 1.9; which end of that he wants is a flying judgement. PUT BACK TO 0.5 the same day, after he flew 0.9: "it is too nose low and too easy to recover from both upright and inverted flat spins. If you increased the directional stability from the fin I would suspect that" - and he was right about the mechanism. This amplifies the whole fin's flow, the UNDEFLECTED fin included, so it is static directional stiffness as much as rudder power, and stiffness is what flattens a spin out and recovers it on its own. It also broke the inverted flat spin, flown his way (a normal inverted spin on right rudder at idle, THEN power and right aileron - InvertedFlatSpinProbe, INV_FLAT=1): 0.5 holds alpha -87.5 at 1.27 s a turn, 0.8 holds -85.7, and 0.9 collapses it to -68.2 at 2.44. A cliff between 0.8 and 0.9, and 0.9 was over it. At 0.5 with the rudder spoiler now carrying the recovery: upright flat alpha 79.5 (his 80 target, against 77.4 at 0.9), 5.74 turns to stop rotating (against 2.86, which he called too easy), inverted flat -87.5. The recovery is affordable at 0.5 only because ControlSpoilerK reaches the rudder now - it was 6.90 turns at 0.5 this morning without it - and that term exists ONLY while a control is deflected, so it buys authority without the stiffness.
spinAero.controlSpoilerKSource: A deflected control on a BROADSIDE surface acts as a spoiler on the separated wake, not as a flap: adds k*sin(delta)*|sin(alpha_chord)|*q*S normal to the FIXED surface, over hinged horizontal-tail strips only, ramped in over 30-50 deg of the strip's own flow angle. FITTED 2026-11-10 to Ty flying a clip of his own Pitts flat spin: "the elevator literally does nothing in the spin. It is almost guaranteed to be elevator authority", and "Pushing the stick forward during a spin accelerates the spin due to conservation of angular momentum". MEASURED BEFORE IT WAS BUILT (ElevatorBreakdownProbe, ELE_BRK=1): the tail is NOT short of air - its strips fly at 68-89 deg of local flow with eta_t 1.16-1.22, MORE dynamic pressure than the free stream, because the tail is swung 3.2 m out on a 4.7 rad/s rotation - and its area and arm are right. The only missing factor is the coefficient: the elevator's whole travel moves Cn by 0.387 at alpha 30 and 0.062 at alpha 80, because post-stall the section law is Cd_max*sin(theta), which is FLAT at broadside. At alpha 80 the elevator was moving 296 N of CHORDWISE force on a 0.07 m arm and 48 N of normal force. So his first instinct - give the stab the fin's crossflow dynamic pressure (StabSidewashK) - could not have worked, and was measured and left at 0. Elevator authority at alpha 80, deg/s2: k 0 -> 3.7, 0.3 -> 15.5, 0.6 -> 27.4, 1.0 -> 43.4 (against 45 at alpha 30, which was already healthy). 0.6 keeps a sensible shape - still less at broadside than at a normal spin's alpha - where 1.0 makes it nearly flat from 30 to 90 deg, which a plate should not be. NOTE IT COSTS SOMETHING: hands-off it makes the Beggs-Mueller recovery SLOWER (6.90 -> 7.53 turns), because the free elevator sits on its aft stop and now holds the spin harder; the fin sidewash going 0.5 -> 0.9 more than pays that back.
spinAero.stabHighAlphaKSource: Multiplier on each horizontal-tail strip's whole force where its own LOCAL angle is 60-90 deg (folded about 90, mirrored for negative alpha, ramped in over 50-60). FITTED 2026-11-09 to the owner's own target, given after he flew 2026.1109.1912: "make the stab more effective 60-90 aoa", "More effective", "Ideally the stability would just barely allow a 85 degree attitude with full power and opposite aileron", "Upright". He then moved the target: "Tweak the stab for 80 nose down not 85". At 1.9 the upright power-on out-spin-aileron flat spin sits at alpha 80.1, nose 9.1 deg down (FlatSpinProbe), and it is still JUST BARELY allowed: take the opposite aileron out and it steepens to 74.2 and slows from 1.24 to 1.47 s a turn, so 80 needs both full power and the aileron. 1.1 held the earlier 85.2 target. Sweep: K 1.0 -> 86.0, 1.1 -> 85.2, 1.2 -> 84.4, 1.3 -> 83.6, 1.4 -> 82.8, 1.8 -> 80.5, 1.9 -> 80.1, 2.0 -> 79.7, 2.5 -> 78.1. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO: it does not recover the spin at ANY value - across K 1.0 to 2.5 the Beggs-Mueller yaw rate after 15 s moves only -4.47 to -4.30 rad/s, because the rudder is dead at every one of those attitudes (0.2 deg/s2 of yaw at alpha 91, 0.9 at 60; SpinAuthorityProbe). The flat-spin RECOVERY is the fin's flat normal force, not the stabiliser. Plate theory has nothing left to give here either - the derived section is already at Cn 1.18-1.19 over 60-90 against Cd_max 1.19 - so this exceeds it on his flight evidence rather than on a reference, which is what the config doc on SpinAeroConfig.StabHighAlphaK says.
spinAero.shadowKSource: Geometric helical shadow depth (TailWake.GeometricShadow): the share of dynamic pressure a fully shadowed strip loses. Replaces the Report 648 wake correlation for EVERY surface of this type. Swept 2026-11-08 against the spin set with the receiver's own chord wired through: 0.3 leaves the full-power upright neutral spin at 88.3 deg, 0.5 puts it at 85.3 which is Ty's 2026-11-03 number (~85, 'just shy of flat'), and 0.7 over-rotates it to 82.0 with the bank growing. At 0.5 every one of the owner's stated figures is met: upright out-spin flat 92.0 / +2.7 against his 95/+5 limit, inverted flat -92.3 / +2.6 inside his 90-95, bank 2-15 against 'not more than 30, probably more like 10', and the polarity he described - upright nose LOW (-3.5) and inverted nose HIGH (+1.6) - falls out of the geometry with no coefficient arranging it. The SHAPE of the model is geometry; this one number is the tunable.
spinAero.controlSpoilerOnsetDegSource: The spoiler ramp starts at the SECTION'S OWN STALL. 30 deg was chosen when every hStab was a naca0012 (stall 14 deg); a flat plate stalls at 9-12, which left alpha 20-34 with no table effectiveness and no spoiler yet - and that band WAS the hole in the elevator authority. Worth the whole difference: authority floor 0.165 at onset 30 against 0.249 at onset 10. Ty 2026-11-10 accepted the plate knowing this moves the term he judged the Pitts' spin on.

propulsion.dryBoundaryExcessSource: Dry boundary friction excess at rest, over the power curve's own running friction intercept (PistonEngine.BoundaryFrictionFactor): 4.71 means this engine resists 5.71x its running friction when it is dead and dry. Lycoming AEIO-540, 541.5 cu in, 6 cyl, CR 8.7. SOLVED 2026-11-10 (lane/claude-boundary-friction, CompressionStopProbe with COMPSTOP=1 SOLVE=1) against Ty's anchor "Cranking resistance should be calibrated such that at fine pitch the prop stops right at level flight stall speed", and then his "fix it per engine": it is the one value that puts the measured stopping speed on this type's OWN stall speed, 29.5 m/s = 66 mph (PracticeScenario.EstimateVso, sea level, flaps up - the number the rest of the suite is tuned against, not a book figure). Solved and not predicted: nothing inside an engine explains the fleet's spread, because motoring friction and rated torque both scale with displacement - see PistonEngine.BoundaryExcessFor for what was tried and rejected. THIS IS NOW THE ONLY THING IN THE DEAD-ENGINE MODEL THAT IS FITTED TO ANYTHING: the compression peak beside it is the engine's own gas load out of its displacement and compression ratio (PistonCompression.PeakNmFor), and the speed a stopped propeller breaks away at is a measurement rather than an anchor. Re-solving moves it about 0.1 because the sweep that measures the stopping speed steps 0.25 m/s. The fleet default for every type not yet solved is 3.0.
propulsion.hubXMSource: Propeller disc station, body x, m. MEASURED: docs/aircraft/pitts-s2b-inertia-DERIVATION.md's part-by-part build-up puts the disc at +1.600 (firewall +0.574, engine 1.026 m long). The derived fallback gave +1.283 - 0.317 m too far aft, because it anchors a spinner-to-tail-post length at the rudder's trailing edge. An earlier placement from the TCDS A8SO arms used +1.68; the build-up is the later and more careful of the two.
propulsion.pitchStopSource: PUBLISHED, not derived: FAA TCDS A8SO Rev 21 gives the Hartzell HC-C2YR-4CF/FC8477A-4 as low 11.0 deg +/-0.1 and high 32-34 deg at the 30 in station, which on a 78-80 in prop is within a whisker of 0.75 R. Taking 33 for the high stop. Ty's two rules (the 26 inHg run-up and no overspeed until Vd) derive 15.36/28.68 for this blade — narrower at BOTH ends, which activity factor alone cannot explain since more blade moves both stops finer. The likely cause is the blade twist law: BladeElement uses constant geometric pitch and a real blade is twisted less than that toward the tip, so its reference-station angle maps differently onto torque. Measured hardware beats a derivation, so the published numbers are used and the rules stay as the method for types with no published data.
propulsion.propInertiaSource: Propeller + spinner + the crank's rotating parts, kg.m2. From the OWNER'S BLADE RULE (2026-11-09, tools/aircraft_builder/prop_inertia.py): each blade is 15 % of the net propeller weight with its centre of mass at 25 % of the DIAMETER from the axis, the rest being hub near the axis - because a heavy constant-speed hub contributes almost nothing to sum(m r^2), so a mass-weighted estimate overstates the couple. M 36.3 kg, D 1.98 m, 2 blades: blades 2.668 + hub 0.254 (k 0.10 m) + crank 0.14 = 3.06, against 3.06 before. MASS: SOURCED: 80 lb, owner data (docs/aircraft/pitts-s2b-inertia-DERIVATION.md). AEIO-540, six cylinders. VALIDATION: the rule reproduces Hartzell's published two-blade polar moment to +18 % (1.412 against 1.198) and runs +60 % high on their three-blade one, so it is applied to two-blade types only.
propulsion.coarseOnOilLossSource: Ty 2026-11-10: "aerobatic aircraft with a constant speed propeller default to high pitch with loss of oil pressure like twins do (Seminole beech 18 etc) and standard single engines default to low pitch with no oil pressure". Oil holds these blades FINE, so losing it drives them COARSE - a twin's path to feather, and on an aerobatic single what stops the prop overspeeding pointed down.
propulsion.normalForceKSource: Propeller in-plane (normal/H) force, PropModel.NormalForce. OFF for this type. The term is real and was absent from the model entirely (every other propeller effect was axial force or a pure moment), and at 0.10 it was worth a slight improvement while the biplane shadow was still wrong. With the geometric helical shadow in (spinAero.shadowK) it over-corrects: 0.10 rolls the full-power inverted spin out into an upright one (alpha +95). Kept at 0 until there is a reason to re-fit it, with the code and its tests in place.
propulsion.thrustLineZSource: Prop axis 0.20 m ABOVE the CG, so thrust is nose-down with power. Was 0, which asserted no offset at all. The body origin IS the thrust line on this fleet - the Extra has cg.z 0 and thrustLineZ 0, consistently - and this type deliberately puts its CG at z +0.20, i.e. below the origin; the Great Lakes has the identical hole at 0.25 and is NOT changed here. Unlike the gyro this does not mirror: nose-down with power upright is nose-UP with respect to the earth inverted, which is Ty's 2026-11-08 observation that 'upright spins are more nose low and inverted flat spins are more nose high'. Inferred from the fleet convention and the gear height, not measured off a drawing.

gear.toeOutDegSource: A standing slip angle on each main, outboard, so the pair cancel when the load is even and restore when it is not: the heavier wheel's outboard side force is the larger one, which pushes the aeroplane back toward the light side and shares the load out again. Ty 2026-11-10, flying both types: "How are the main gear tires aligned? It acts like it has toe in" - they were dead straight, which is the one thing a sprung taildragger's gear never is - then "Try 1 degree toe out both sides", and the mechanism in his own words: "The loaded tire tries to unload back to the other". 1.0 deg is his number, not a fitted one. The sign comes from the wheel's own y, so one value on both mains means outboard on both (LandingGear.ToeRad).
gear.gearTypeSource: Rubber shock cord, in the belly, loaded through the legs -- Ty 2026-11-10: "the pitts bungees are in the belly and the cabana struts attach to them so cabana pulls on bungee inside" (the model draws the spool and the cord wraps: Gear_Bungee, Gear_Bungee_Housing). The same KIND of spring as the Cub's in a different place, so it is the same word here, with its own geometry.
gear.legPivotSource: Measured off pitts-s2b-like-own.glb (Gear_Main): the A-frame pick-ups leave the lower longerons at span 0.22, up -0.570 (the leg mesh's highest point at that span; build_pitts_s2b.py puts them there from the Aviat three-view and the VH-ZZZ head-on photo), and the tyre touches at span 0.81, up -1.329. 0.59 m out, 0.759 m down: splay 1.29. The front and rear pick-ups are at the same y, so the hinge they make is fore-and-aft and the wheel swings in the frame's plane.

loading._comment: seats[].eye is the seated pilot's EYE (owner Ty, approved 2026-10-31), body frame +x fwd, +y right, +z DOWN, measured on extended gear; the Cockpit camera sits exactly there. The PRIMARY seat is first. loading.seats[].station, loading.tanks[] and loading.baggage[] are the arms from docs/pending/loading-arm-estimates.md (Codex lane, 2026-11-01): a published TCDS/POH arm where the row is CONFIRMED, converted to this frame through that aircraft's anchor. maxKg is the published placard where the source gives one. referenceKg is UNCHANGED and still follows the 172's convention, so the reference loading reproduces the authored mass, CG and inertia exactly and nothing moves at spawn. Whether each airframe's authored massKg includes a pilot or fuel is still the open W&B decision in AGENT-LOG NEEDS YOU.
loading._seatPlacardNote: maxKg is a CONVENTIONAL occupant placard (250 lb, and the J-3's own authored 300 lb), not a figure read from a POH. referenceKg follows the 172's convention: the primary seat carries the pilot that mass.massKg already includes, so the reference loading still reproduces the authored mass, CG and inertia exactly and nothing moves at spawn. Whether each airframe's authored massKg really includes a pilot is the open W&B decision in AGENT-LOG NEEDS YOU.
